questions.question: How do inheritance and `super()` work in Python?
questions.title: Python Inheritance and super()
questions.direct_answer: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and specialize behaviour from a base class. `super()` follows the method resolution order to call the next implementation, which supports cooperative initialization and overriding.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand inherited lookup, overriding, and why `super()` is better than hard-coding a parent call.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing `super()` as simply the parent object or forgetting to initialize required base state.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State that `super()` follows MRO and therefore supports cooperative multiple inheritance.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A subclass inherits attributes and methods from its base classes.
A subclass can override an inherited method with its own definition.
`super()` returns a proxy that continues lookup after the current class in the MRO.
A subclass initializer often calls `super().__init__` for base state.
Use inheritance for a genuine substitutable is-a relationship.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Inheritance creates a new class from one or more base classes. If an attribute is not defined on the subclass, Python can continue searching its base classes. The subclass may also override a method when it needs specialized behaviour.

`super()` is a proxy for continuing that lookup after the current class according to the method resolution order. It is commonly used in a subclass initializer so the base class can create the state it owns. It is more accurate than thinking of `super()` as one fixed parent.

For example, `Employee.__init__` can call `super().__init__(name)` to let `Person` set `name`, then add `employee_id`. An overridden `describe` method can build on `super().describe()` instead of repeating the person's formatting.

A direct call such as `Person.__init__(self, name)` can work in a simple hierarchy, but it hard-codes one class and may skip other cooperative classes in multiple inheritance. Inheritance is most suitable when every subclass can be used wherever the base contract is expected. If the relationship is only has-a, composition is usually clearer.

sections.title: Lookup and initialization move through a hierarchy
sections.content:
A derived class stores references to its bases. Normal attribute lookup uses the class's method resolution order, so inherited behaviour is available without being copied into the subclass. Defining the same name in the subclass changes which implementation is found first.

Base initializers do not run merely because a subclass exists. When the base owns required state, the subclass should participate in its initialization contract. A cooperative method accepts the arguments it owns, calls `super()` appropriately, and allows the next class in the ordering to do the same.

Subtype design matters more than code reuse. A subtype should preserve the expectations of code written for the base type. If `Report` merely contains a `Formatter`, making `Report` inherit from `Formatter` would claim the wrong relationship. Delegating to a contained formatter keeps responsibilities independent and easier to replace.

sections.title: A cooperative subclass initializer
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[Employee Mina E-7] --> E[Employee.__init__]
  E --> S[super().__init__ name]
  S --> P[Person.__init__ sets name]
  P --> B[Return to Employee]
  B --> I[Set employee_id]
```

questions.question: What is method resolution order (MRO) in Python?
questions.title: Python MRO and Multiple Inheritance
questions.direct_answer: MRO is the ordered list Python follows when looking for methods and other class attributes. In multiple inheritance, C3 linearization produces a consistent order that respects local base ordering and visits each class once.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can reason about overlapping inherited methods and cooperative `super()` calls.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling MRO a simple depth-first search or assuming `super()` always names the class written first in the bases.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace a diamond once and inspect `Class.__mro__` rather than guessing.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: MRO defines the lookup order for a class and all its bases.
Python uses C3 linearization for a consistent, monotonic order.
Zero-argument `super()` continues from the current class along that order.
Cooperative methods let every class in a diamond run once.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Method resolution order is the sequence Python searches for an attribute on a class hierarchy. It begins with the requested class, continues through its bases in a calculated order, and ends at `object`. The order can be inspected with `Class.__mro__` or `Class.mro()`.

It matters most with multiple inheritance. Python uses C3 linearization, which preserves the left-to-right precedence declared by classes, keeps parent ordering consistent in subclasses, and does not visit the same class twice. A hierarchy that cannot satisfy these rules is rejected when the class is created.

For example, if `Combined(LoggingMixin, BaseService)` defines no `save`, lookup checks `Combined`, then follows its printed MRO. A call to `super().save()` inside `LoggingMixin` continues to the next class in that same order rather than jumping to a fixed parent.

This lets a diamond hierarchy use cooperative methods: each implementation performs its part and delegates onward, so a shared base runs once. The boundary is that participating methods need compatible signatures and consistent `super()` use. Multiple inheritance is best kept to small, focused mixins because state-heavy hierarchies are difficult to reason about.

sections.title: Linearizing a diamond without repeating its base
sections.content:
Imagine `ReportService` inheriting from `AuditMixin` and `Service`, while both eventually lead to `object`. There are multiple paths through the graph, but attribute lookup needs one line. C3 produces that line while keeping each class ahead of its own parents and respecting the bases listed by the developer.

`super()` is designed for this linear path. In a method defined by `AuditMixin`, it begins after `AuditMixin` in the MRO of the actual receiver's class. That next class can differ depending on which final class combines the mixin. This is why calling a base class by name and calling `super()` do not mean exactly the same thing.

Cooperative multiple inheritance works when each participant performs one responsibility, accepts compatible arguments, and delegates exactly once. If one class stops the chain or directly invokes a shared base, work may be skipped or duplicated. Printing the MRO turns an otherwise abstract problem into an exact trace.

sections.title: Diamond graph and its single lookup path
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  C[Combined] --> L[LoggingMixin]
  C --> S[Service]
  L --> B[Base]
  S --> B
  B --> O[object]
  P[Lookup path] --> Q[Combined → LoggingMixin → Service → Base → object]
```
